title: Vocabulary: social awareness
keyIdea: Eight words help you talk about how people are treated. A stereotype is a fixed idea about a whole group. Prejudice is judging one person before you know them, because of their group. Discrimination is treating someone unfairly because of their group: it is an action. Bias is a leaning for or against someone, often without noticing. Equality means everyone gets the same; equity means everyone gets what they need for a fair chance. Fairness is treating people in a right and even way, with no favourites. Compassion is noticing someone is hurting and wanting to help.

kid: Some words help us talk about how people are treated. They are close in meaning, so it helps to know what makes each one different.

Start with think, feel, do. A stereotype is an idea about a whole group, like "girls can't play football." Prejudice is when you judge one person by that idea before you know them. Discrimination is when you do something unfair to them, like keep them off the team.

Equality means everyone gets the same thing. Equity means each person gets what they need to have a fair chance. If one child needs glasses to read the board, giving her glasses is equity. Fairness means the rules are the same for all, with no favourites.

Bias is a leaning for or against a group. People often have it and don't know it. You spot it as a pattern, not from one time. Compassion is when you see that someone is sad or hurt, care about it, and want to help.
adult: This topic is for ages 7 to 11. It gives children words for what they see in the playground, in stories and in the news. The words are close in meaning, so the aim is to know what sets each apart. A stereotype is a belief about a group. Prejudice is judging a person before you know them. Discrimination is unfair treatment: it is an action. Bias is a lean in judgement that people may not notice. Equality is the same for all; equity is what each person needs for a fair chance.

In the lab, children sort sayings into think (stereotype), judge (prejudice) and do (discrimination). They share three boxes behind a fence so three children of different heights can all see a match. They flip a judge's scores until a pattern of bias shows. They pick a kind way to help someone who is left out or hurt. Last, they match eight short scenes to the eight words.

Common mistakes: using discrimination for any unkind thought (it needs an action), and calling every stereotype prejudice. Some children think equity is unfair because it is not equal. Others decide a person is biased from one choice, not a pattern. Another slip is thinking compassion is just feeling sorry; it also means wanting to help.
Use the words when they come up in a book or a match. Ask: "Was that a stereotype, or did someone get treated differently?"

familyTip: When you watch a programme or read a story together, pause on a moment where someone is judged or left out and ask your child which word fits best: stereotype, prejudice, discrimination or bias. Ask what a fair or kind response would be.

practice.prompt: "All teenagers are lazy." Which word is this?
practice.hint: Is it an idea about a whole group, or something that was done?
practice.explain: It is a fixed idea about a whole group, so it is a stereotype. Nobody has been treated differently yet, so it is not discrimination.

practice.prompt: A club turns away {n} children only because of their religion. Which word is this?
practice.hint: Did someone just think something, or did they do something?
practice.explain: The children were treated unfairly because of their group. That is an action, so it is discrimination, not only prejudice.

practice.prompt: {n} children get one cushion each, but Ana is much shorter and still can't see the stage. What would equity look like?
choices: Give Ana what she needs to see
Ask Ana to stand at the back
practice.hint: Equity is about what each person needs for a fair chance.
practice.explain: Equal cushions did not give Ana a fair chance to see. Equity gives her what she needs, such as an extra cushion or a front seat.

practice.prompt: A judge gives one team a lower score once. Can you be sure the judge is biased?
choices: No, you need to see a pattern
practice.hint: One result could have many reasons. What would show a leaning?
practice.explain: Bias shows up as a pattern over many decisions. One low score might have a fair reason.

practice.prompt: Leo sees a new girl sitting alone. Which shows compassion?
choices: He asks her to join his game
He feels sorry for her and walks on
practice.hint: Compassion is noticing, caring and wanting to help.
practice.explain: Asking her to join shows Leo noticed she was alone, cared, and acted to help. Feeling sorry and walking on is only the start.

pool.prompt: Ella decides the new boy will be unkind before she has even met him, because of where he is from. Which word is this?
pool.hint: Is she judging one person, or stating an idea about a group?
pool.explain: Ella is judging one person before she knows him, because of his group. That is prejudice.

pool.prompt: Which one is an action, not just a thought?
pool.hint: Think, feel, do. Which word is the do?
pool.explain: Discrimination is treating someone unfairly. A stereotype is an idea and prejudice is a judgement; both can stay in someone's head.

pool.prompt: Every child in the class gets {n} stickers, whatever they did. Which word is this?
pool.hint: Did everyone get the same, or did people get different amounts by need?
pool.explain: Everyone got exactly the same, so this is equality.

pool.prompt: Sam uses a wheelchair, so the school builds a ramp. Which word is this?
pool.hint: Did Sam get the same as everyone, or what he needs?
pool.explain: The ramp gives Sam what he needs to get in, like everyone else. Giving by need is equity.

pool.prompt: Over {n} lessons, a teacher always picks boys to answer and does not notice. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Is there a pattern of leaning one way, even if no one meant it?
pool.explain: A leaning towards one group that shows as a pattern, often without noticing, is bias.

pool.prompt: Which is the best meaning of compassion?
choices: Noticing someone is hurting and wanting to help
pool.hint: It has two parts: noticing, and wanting to help.
pool.explain: Compassion means you notice someone is suffering and want to help them. Feeling sorry alone is not the whole thing.

pool.prompt: In a game, the same rules apply to every team, and the ref has no favourites. Which word is this?
pool.hint: Are people treated in a right and even way?
pool.explain: Same rules for all and no favourites is fairness.

pool.prompt: "Boys don't cry." Nobody has done anything yet. Is this discrimination?
pool.hint: Is there an action yet, or only an idea about a group?
pool.explain: It is an idea about a whole group, so it is a stereotype. It would become discrimination if someone was treated unfairly because of it.

visual.caption: Think, feel or do? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: judging the new boy before meeting him
deciding you won't like someone because of their accent
not letting someone join because of their skin colour
paying a woman less for the same job

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort think, feel and do; share boxes behind a fence; flip a judge's scores to spot bias; choose a compassionate action; then name eight scenes.
